newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia privatisation not to discourage investors.
newsitem.headline: Serbia privatisation not to discourage investors.

text.p: Serbia, criticised for slow progress on economic reforms, presented on Thursday a final version of its draft privatisation law to become effective from October 31, 1997.
"This is the best and the most modern law ever made in a transition economy," Serbian Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic told Reuters.

The law, substantially changed from its first draft, falls short of voucher privatisation used in other former communist economies. The government aims to have 80 percent of companies sold within two years.

It also does not tackle restitution of property seized under communism seen as too complex and requiring at least three to four years to disentangle. The law excludes the unemployed, Yugoslavs working abroad and immediate heirs.

"There is no absolute fairness with a law like this. Our intentions were sincere, but to include all those people would be technically difficult. It will also create difficulties in implementing reforms in the Serbian economy," Privatisation Minister Milan Beko told reporters.
"We do not want to be reformists in words, we want to be reformists in our deeds," Beko told Reuters.

Beko helped the government obtain almost $1 billion through the sale of a 49 percent stake in Telekom Srbija to Stet of Italy and OTE of Greece. He was confident Serbia would soon attract more foreign funds.
The minister insisted the strategic partnership with Stet and OTE was not a lifebelt for politicians but an impetus for development and an encouragement for other foreign investment.
He sought foreign support for Serbia's reforms, more foreign funds and external help for the country's return to the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
Dragan Djuricin, an economist, said privatisation focused on employees would not necessarily discourage investors or bring back the self-management system of the communist era.
"There is a stereotype that an insider privatisation will bring back self-management, but it is incorrect to claim that it would be impossible to attract foreign capital," he said.

Investors can obtain control over a company much more easily now that the number of shareholders is so big. "With dispersed ownership, controlling stake can be obtained already with 10-25 percent of shares," Djuricin said.

Beko, also a director of a private company, said: "Speaking as a private investor and a businessman, I think we must accept all mechanisms of a market economy and this process in Serbia will allow investors to acquire a controlling stake in firms at a much lower level.
"We shall create domestic capital market, and there will be possibilities for investors to enter privatisation through the bourse, banks and the Serbian Share Fund," he said.
Beko also defended the privatisation law for not being compulsory for companies.
"The state did not want to force all companies to transform and privatise at once, for that would create a stampede. But in two years 80 percent of all companies will be transformed."

The economy, working at close to 40 percent of its capacity and with almost 50 percent of labour out of work, was not seen capable of absorbing at once the entire 100 billion German marks ($58 billion) in socially-owned capital to be privatised.
"That is why this capital will be released to the market gradually, along with the economy increasing its absorbency," said Beko.

The privatisation law will offer a partial relaxation to the problem of over $4 billion in frozen hard currency savings. Holders of those deposits will be issued state bonds and allowed to buy shares with the bonds' face value.
"The law intends to bring a substantial relaxation to the problem but the state will have to secure additional sources to service the debt," Beko said.
Privatisation will be followed by a bank overhaul programme planned to breathe life into the ailing financial sector.
